newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - March 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - March 21.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company

-- BARCLAYS PAY 'RIP-OFF' Barclays Bank has been accused of trying to push through "rip off" changes in pay policy by its staff union. The changes, which will reduce 13 clerical and managerial grades into seven bands and change existing contract of employment terms,have provided the focal point for opposition from the Union for Barclays Staff, which represents 45,000 employees and pensioners. The union claims that the changes will leave many staff without much hope of promotion or rise in salary.

-- OCEAN AIMS TO EXPAND AFTER OIL DISPOSAL The freight management group, Ocean, will use the profits from its disposal of OIL, the offshore oil platforms services business, to expand in global freight management. A profit of 228 million pounds stg from the 328 million pounds stg sale of OIL to Tidewater of New Orleans will help further Ocean's goal of becoming a world leader in global logistics, a value-added freight service. Ocean's shares rose 26 to 535.5p on Thursday, a five-year high.

-- THOUSANDS SWELL CO-OP NUMBER Thousands of 1 pound stg membership applications have been made to the Co-operative movement since reports that Andrew Regan, who wants to buy the Co-op's non-food businesses, will offer 1,000 pounds stg for members votes. Tuesday's edition of the Co-op movement's newspaper, Co-operative News, reports that the Co-operative Retail Society had been signing up to 1,000 new members a day.

-- SHARES TUMBLE AS GREENSPAN OVERSHADOWS INFLATION FALL Shares in London suffered their biggest daily loss since December following a warning of higher American interest rates by Alan Greenspan, Chairman of the US Federal Reserve. The FT-SE 100 index closed on Thursday 74.1 points down at 4,258.1, which is 186 points lower than its all-time high on March 11. The selling came despite news that British retail price inflation fell in February.

-- LEGAL & GENERAL OFFERS 'MIS-SELLING' SOLUTION Legal & General claims to have a solution to help the half a million people who were sold personal pension plans after being tempted out of their occupational schemes. The insurer is proposing to issue a legally binding guarantee to restore any loss of benefits to pension plan holders wrongly advised by L&G representatives to opt out of their company scheme, and have earmarked an unspecified proportion of the group's 20 billion pounds stg life fund to back the guarantees.

-- COURTAULDS PROFIT DEPLETED BY COSTS OF CUTTING ITS CLOTH Profits at Courtaulds Textiles were almost wiped out for 1996 due to the cost of re-organisation. After exceptional charges, pre-tax profits for the year to the end of December were 400,000 pounds, compared with 36.5 million pounds stg in pre-tax profits for 1995. Exceptional costs for 1996 were 31.7 million pounds stg covering the cost of reductions in existing businesses and shifting of manufacturing abroad.

-- EXPORTS FALL TO 3-YEAR LOW Sterling's strength against competitor currencies has lowered export demand for UK manufactured goods to its lowest level in three years. The figures being announced on Friday in the Confederation of British Industry's latest report will show that the strength of the pound is beginning to take its toll on export orders, but an improved demand for domestic goods has more than compensated for the fall in exports.

-- TESCO SEEKS 600 MILLION POUNDS IRISH SHOPPING BASKET Tesco announced on Thursday it is in ongoing talks to buy the Irish supermarket chains owned by Associated British Foods. The deal, thought to be worth 600 million pounds stg, is expected to include the Republic of Ireland's largest food retailer, Quinnsworth, as well as Crazy Prices and Stewarts, the Northern Irish retailers.

-- NAT EXPRESS CUTS RAIL JOBS AND RAISES PROFITS National Express, the coach and train operator revealed on Thursday a sharp 45 percent rise in pre-tax profits to 60.1 million pounds stg, and a 15 percent increase in dividends to shareholders. The company also announced that it had cut nearly one fifth of the staff at Midland Mainline and Gatwick Express, the first two rail franchises it won, amounting to 325 job losses. National Express refused to say whether there would be job cuts at its other three rail franchises.

-- LIGGETT TO SETTLE US TOBACCO LAWSUITS The Liggett Group, maker of Chesterfield cigarettes, is poised to acknowledge formally that smoking is addictive and can cause cancer. The group, the smallest of the main US tobacco companies, is expected to confirm it has negotiated an agreement to settle lawsuits filed against the industry by 22 US states and in return it would gain immunity in the future from such lawsuits.

-- NORWICH TO HAND OUT 3 BILLION POUNDS WINDFALL Norwich Union will give around 1.8 million with-profits policy holders an estimated 720 pounds stg when the mutual insurance giant floats in June. The share allocation is more generous and wider than anticipated, although several million policy holders with household or motor insurance polices will not be included in the bonanza. The basis for calculating the handout has not been published, but there is no maximum award.
-- GUINNESS WARNS OF 100 MILLION POUNDS HIT FROM STERLING

Guinness has warned that the soaring pound would hit its 1997 profits by 60 million pounds stg with a further 40 million pounds stg hit next year if sterling maintained its current strength. The warning took the shine off full year results that showed a return to growth after years of stagnation. Profit before tax of 975 million pounds stg was pegged back by the extra interest paid on borrowings to fund last year's buy back of 5 percent of Guinness's shares, otherwise profits would have been over 1 billion pounds stg for the first time.
